summary: Specifies TCP-Friendly Rate Control, a congestion control mechanism for unicast flows in best-effort networks. It shares bandwidth fairly with TCP but varies throughput much less over time, which suits telephony and streaming media. It was replaced by RFC 5348.

eli5.summary: TCP slows down and speeds up in jumps. TFRC changes speed gently, like a car cruising steadily, while still sharing the road fairly. It was later replaced by RFC 5348.

questions: how does tfrc differ from tcp
what is the tfrc throughput equation
subtitle: A congestion control mechanism that shares bandwidth fairly with TCP but changes its sending rate smoothly.

tldr.problem: TCP halves its sending rate on a single packet drop, which makes throughput jumpy and a poor fit for telephony or streaming media that want a smooth rate.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver measures the loss event rate and reports it back. The sender measures round-trip time and plugs both into a TCP throughput equation to get its allowed rate.
tldr.outcome: TFRC stays reasonably fair to TCP with much lower variation in throughput, but reacts more slowly to changes. RFC 3448 has since been obsoleted by RFC 5348.

facts.label: Fairness target
facts.value: Within a factor of two of TCP

today: RFC 3448 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 5348, which is the current TFRC specification.

sections.title: Why a Smoother Congestion Controller
sections.content:
TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC) is a congestion control mechanism for unicast flows in a best-effort Internet. It is not a full protocol: it does not define packet formats or reliability. It is meant to be used inside a transport protocol such as RTP, in an application that does its own end-to-end congestion control, or with endpoint congestion management.

TFRC is reasonably fair to TCP, which the RFC defines as a sending rate generally within a factor of two of a TCP flow under the same conditions. Its throughput varies much less over time, which suits telephony and streaming media. The price is that it responds more slowly than TCP to changes in available bandwidth.

The RFC says TFRC should only be used when an application needs smooth throughput. For applications that just want to move as much data as fast as possible, it recommends TCP. TFRC is also for applications with a fixed packet size that vary packets per second; a variant for fixed-rate, variable-size audio, TFRC-PS, was left to a later document.
sections.eli5: Some programs, like phone calls, hate sudden speed changes. TFRC gives them a calm, steady speed that still plays fair with everyone else.

sections.title: The Throughput Equation
sections.content:
TFRC feeds the loss event rate and the round-trip time into a formula that approximates how fast a TCP flow would go, then sends at that rate. A loss event is one or more lost or marked packets from a window of data; a marked packet is a congestion signal from ECN.

The recommended equation is a slightly simplified version of the one for Reno TCP. It gives the transmit rate X in bytes per second from the packet size s, the round-trip time R, the loss event rate p (between 0 and 1.0), the TCP retransmission timeout t_RTO and b, the number of packets acknowledged by one TCP acknowledgement.

The RFC simplifies further by setting t_RTO = 4*R and recommends b = 1, because many TCP implementations do not use delayed acknowledgements. Other TCP equations may be substituted in future, as long as they reasonably approximate conformant TCP congestion control.
sections.eli5: There is a recipe that says how fast a well-behaved TCP would go if packets are getting lost this often and the trip takes this long. TFRC just follows that recipe.

sections.title: What the Sender Does
sections.content:
The sender starts with X at 1 packet per second and a nofeedback timer of 2 seconds. Each data packet carries a sequence number, a timestamp and the sender's current round-trip time estimate. Each feedback packet from the receiver carries the timestamp of the last data packet received, the delay before the report was generated, the receive rate X_recv and the loss event rate p.

When feedback arrives, the sender computes a round-trip sample, smooths it with a filter constant q (default 0.9) and sets t_RTO = 4*R. If p is above zero, the new rate is the calculated rate limited to at most twice X_recv. If p is zero, the sender is in slow-start and roughly doubles its rate each round-trip time.

If no feedback arrives before the nofeedback timer expires, the sender cuts its rate in half. The maximum back-off interval, t_mbi, is 64 seconds, so the sender sends at least one packet every 64 seconds while p is above zero.

Two optional or practical details follow. An optional adjustment reduces the rate as queuing delay rises, which helps when few flows share a link. A sending loop also schedules each packet from the previous nominal send time, so the average rate holds even when the operating system timer is coarse.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps asking the receiver how things are going and adjusts its speed. If the receiver goes quiet for too long, the sender slows down to half speed to be safe.

sections.title: What the Receiver Does
sections.content:
The receiver measures the loss event rate. It decides a packet is lost when at least three packets with higher sequence numbers have arrived, the same rule TCP uses to cope with reordering. A late packet can still fill the hole and the rate is recomputed. For ECN-capable connections, a marked packet counts as a congestion event as soon as it arrives. A retransmission must get a new sequence number.

Losses within one round-trip time are grouped into a single loss event, much as TCP halves its window only once per round-trip time. The receiver then averages the most recent loss intervals with weights; for n=8 the weights are 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2. The loss event rate is p = 1 / I_mean. The RFC says TFRC should not be used with n significantly greater than 8 for traffic competing with TCP on the global Internet.

Feedback should normally go out at least once per round-trip time, and immediately when a new loss event is detected. An optional history discounting mechanism lets the receiver respond more quickly to a sudden absence of congestion. After the first loss, the receiver seeds its history with a synthetic interval chosen so the equation gives a rate within 5% of X_recv.
sections.eli5: The receiver counts how often packets go missing and tells the sender. It lumps together a burst of losses as one bad moment, so one bump in the road does not make the sender panic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TFRC is not a transport protocol itself, so security mostly depends on the transport protocol it is used with. The RFC names two worries. Spoofed feedback could be used for denial of service, so feedback should only be accepted from the receiver of the data. A greedy receiver could also claim to have received packets that were really lost, in order to get more than its fair share of bandwidth.

Possible defenses include a nonce the receiver must feed back to prove receipt. The RFC expects protocols that combine ECN with TFRC to want the ECN nonce, and leaves the details to the transport protocol. A sender-based variant, which would avoid trusting the receiver's loss calculation, is discussed but not specified.
sections.eli5: A cheater could lie about what arrived so the sender goes faster than it should. The fix is to ask for proof, which depends on the protocol around TFRC.

messages.label: Data packet
messages.note: Sequence number, timestamp, sender's RTT estimate.

messages.label: Feedback packet
messages.note: Loss event rate p, receive rate X_recv, timestamp echo and delay.

messages.label: Data at new rate
messages.note: Rate set from the throughput equation, at most 2*X_recv.
